common_name: Aunt Mary's Sweet Corn (Ohio Heirloom White Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost danger has passed, in blocks of short rows for reliable wind pollination on these tall stalks.

directions: Stewarded by an Ohio farm family since before 1850, this open-pollinated white corn was once marketed as one of the finest white sweet corns available. Stalks reach 6-8 feet and typically carry one to two ears with eight to twelve rows of large, deep kernels that turn rich and creamy when cooked, with sweetness varying somewhat ear to ear. Because it needs a full season to fill out, give it consistent moisture and nitrogen through tasseling, and plant in blocks rather than single rows for full ears. Its Midwestern farmhouse pedigree makes it a good choice for gardeners wanting to grow and save a genuinely old regional corn.

common_name: Orchard Baby Sweet Corn (Compact Canadian Heirloom Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger passes; its short stalks and quick maturity suit close spacing, raised beds, and large containers.

directions: Bred in Canada and introduced commercially in the 1940s by a North Dakota seed house, this extra-dwarf sweet corn nearly disappeared after the original seed house closed before being rescued and preserved by heirloom growers. Stalks stand a compact 3 to 5 feet yet still carry two ears each, with small five- to six-inch ears bearing eight to ten rows of tender yellow kernels and old-fashioned, mildly sweet flavor rather than the intense sweetness of modern hybrids. Its short stature and fast finish make it one of the better sweet corns for small gardens, raised beds, or large patio containers. Because it is open-pollinated, isolate it from other corn varieties if you intend to save true seed.

common_name: Tuxana Sweet Corn (Open-Source White Sweet Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; plant in blocks for pollination and give the full-season plants room to reach their mature height.

directions: Tuxana is a modern, open-pollinated white sweet corn developed in southern Oregon by stabilizing a cross between an Anasazi flour corn landrace and a sugary-enhanced hybrid, now maintained and distributed as an Open Source Seed Initiative-pledged variety. Seven-foot stalks generally produce two eight-inch ears with twelve to sixteen rows of large, deep kernels that cook up rich, creamy, and sweet without the cloying intensity of supersweet hybrids. Because it breeds true, gardeners can save seed year to year, making it a good option for anyone wanting hybrid-level ear quality in a variety they can maintain themselves. Isolate from other corn types at pollination time to keep seed pure.

common_name: Sherwood Red Okra (Red Okra 98, Tennessee Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm; this fast-growing Tennessee heirloom tolerates the long, humid summers of the Gulf Coast well.

directions: Donated to Southern Exposure Seed Exchange by a Tennessee grower in the late 1970s, this fast-growing, non-prickly okra bears fat, four-inch red-and-green pods on plants with striking red stems and leaf veins. Its low mucilage keeps pods tender even when allowed to grow larger than most varieties, which forgives a missed picking day or two during peak summer harvest. The colorful pods are excellent fried and add both color and mild flavor when sliced raw and young into salads. As with most heirloom okras, its color fades toward green once cooked, but the ornamental red-tinged plants remain a garden standout all season.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is warm; this slow-starting variety rewards the Gulf Coast's long, hot frost-free season with months of continuous production on very tall plants.

directions: Known in Ghana as tall okra, this West African heirloom can tower 8 to 12 feet given a long enough hot season, making it one of the largest okras a gardener can grow. Red-tinged stems and huge, tender leaves top a slow-starting plant that, once established, produces thick-walled, deep green pods often tinged with red continuously until frost. Beyond the pods, its large leaves are traditionally cooked like a mucilaginous spinach among cooks in West Africa. In frost-free tropical climates it behaves as a short-lived woody perennial for years, but in a zone 9a garden it is best grown as a single tall-season annual with plenty of room to spread.

common_name: Brown Dutch Lettuce (Historic Dutch Heirloom Loose-Leaf Lettuce)

planting.note: Direct sow shallowly in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; lettuce seed needs light to germinate well.

directions: One of the oldest documented lettuce names in cultivation, Brown Dutch appears in print as early as the 1740s in English gardening manuals and was carried by American colonial and nineteenth-century gardeners as a reliable cool-season green. It forms a loose, nonheading rosette of large, floppy, deep lime-green leaves with ruffled edges that take on a bronzy pink-brown tinge in cool weather or bright sun, making it as ornamental as it is edible. The old-fashioned, tender leaves have a mild flavor and hold up reasonably well to light frost and summer heat compared with tighter heading types. Because it is open-pollinated and easy to save, it remains a good choice for gardeners wanting to grow a genuinely centuries-old lettuce.
sources: William Woys Weaver - Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

planting.note: Direct sow shallowly in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; keep soil consistently moist while the head forms.

directions: Salamander was among the most widely grown lettuces of the nineteenth century, a black-seeded cabbaging type that forms a dense head of thick, heavily savoyed, deep green leaves. Its crinkled leaf texture and firm heart gave it good heat tolerance for its era, letting nineteenth-century gardeners hold it in the garden longer than many delicate butterheads of the time. The mature heads have a satisfying crunch and mild flavor typical of old cabbage-type lettuces, distinct from the smoother butterheads more common today. It is a worthwhile variety for gardeners wanting to taste a lettuce type that has largely fallen out of modern seed catalogs.
sources: William Woys Weaver - Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

planting.note: Direct sow shallowly in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; this large old crisphead needs a bit more room than compact lettuces.

directions: According to family tradition, this lettuce was grown for generations by a Maryland farm family before a Philadelphia seed house introduced it commercially around 1870. It forms a large, light green head of curly, fringed leaves around a crisp white heart, giving it the crunch of a crisphead with more cold tolerance and less fuss than modern iceberg types. A classic nineteenth-century French gardening reference even illustrated and described the variety, evidence of how far its reputation traveled. Its large old-fashioned heads are well suited to slicing for sandwiches, and it holds in the garden respectably before bolting.
sources: William Woys Weaver - Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

common_name: Early Curled Simpson Lettuce (Silesia, Historic Overwintering Loose-Leaf)

planting.note: Direct sow shallowly as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in fall for overwintering under a cold frame or light mulch in mild climates.

directions: Descended from the French heirloom Silesia and known by several names over the years, including Curled Silesia and White-Seeded Simpson, this loose-leaf lettuce came into wider American use in the 1850s as a quicker-maturing alternative to older sorts. It forms a tight, quick-growing bunch of light green, crumpled leaves about a foot across, without ever forming a true head. Exceptionally cold-hardy, it was traditionally the lettuce of choice for overwintering in cold frames or under straw mulch, shrugging off hard freezes that would kill tenderer types. Its speed and hardiness make it a good pick for the earliest spring salads or a late fall planting pushed into winter.
sources: William Woys Weaver - Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

planting.note: Direct sow shallowly in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop.

directions: Documented as far back as an 1837 English gardening magazine, Tomhannock traces to French seed distributed through the London Horticultural Society but became far more popular in American gardens than in England. Nineteenth-century American seedsmen sold the same lettuce under other names as well. It forms a butterhead-type, somewhat savoyed and blistered head of medium green leaves with distinctive reddish-brown speckling, giving it a decorative look beyond its eating quality. This old dual-purpose butterhead is a good option for gardeners wanting a lettuce with genuine nineteenth-century American roots.
sources: William Woys Weaver - Heirloom Vegetable Gardening
